column2: preproperation — giving up on plans prematurely (Q0 expl., Core Idea, Q2 answer/expl., Explainer para 3)
column5: O'Donoghue & Rabin 1999 AER abstract (https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:aea:aecrev:v:89:y:1999:i:1:p:103-124): naifs procrastinate immediate-cost tasks and preproperate (do too soon) immediate-reward tasks; sophistication mitigates procrastination but exacerbates preproperation
column6: Core Idea parenthetical now "act even sooner on tasks whose rewards are immediate"; Q0 explanation redefines preproperation as doing too early and drops "beneficial accidental persistence"; Q2 answer and explanation rewritten to the immediate-reward preproperation result; Explainer "premature abandonment" replaced by preproperation sentence (same error repeated)

column2: accepting an unfair offer recruits the dlPFC ... accepting unfairness requires actively overriding an emotional rejection response
column5: Knoch et al. 2006 Science 314:829 (https://boris.unibe.ch/61203): disrupting right dlPFC reduces rejection of unfair offers while fairness judgments stay; so dlPFC supports resisting the temptation to accept. Text contradicted its own next sentence
column6: Rewrote para 4 dlPFC sentences: unfair offers activate dlPFC; early reading was override-to-accept; TMS evidence points the other way; dlPFC helps override self-interest to enforce fairness

column2: beta between 0.6 and 0.9, meaning people treat the present as 10-40% more valuable
column5: Arithmetic: 1/0.9=1.11, 1/0.6=1.67; 10-40% is 1-beta. Range 0.6-0.9 consistent with meta-analyses (Cheung, Tymula & Wang: money ~0.82-0.94, non-money ~0.66-0.75; https://www.iza.org/publications/dp/14625/quasi-hyperbolic-present-bias-a-meta-analysis)
column6: 10-40% more valuable -> "roughly 1.1 to 1.7 times as valuable ... (1/beta)"; beta range kept

column2: Typical estimates of beta range from 0.5 to 0.8 (conflicts with intertemporal 0.6-0.9)
column5: Meta-analyses put money beta ~0.82-0.94 and non-money ~0.66-0.75 (IZA DP 14625; Management Science meta-analysis https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=5222564); 0.5-0.8 sits below the money estimates and contradicts the sister page
column6: Now "vary by study and domain, typically between about 0.6 and 0.9 (lower for non-money rewards such as effort or food) ... roughly 1.1x to 1.7x"

column6: US OIRA -> "the US Social and Behavioral Sciences Team"

column2: Q2 expl.: "opt-out systems ... have donation rates near 90%, while opt-in countries have rates near 15%"
column5: Johnson & Goldstein 2003 plot effective consent rates, not donations; actual donation gap is much smaller (https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2018/08/presumed-consent-wales-falls-short.html); same file set's default-effects.md gives opt-out 86-100%, opt-in 4-28%
column6: Now "effective consent rates above 85%, while opt-in countries have consent rates below 30% (Johnson and Goldstein, 2003). Actual donation rates differ far less, because consent is only one step toward donation."

column2: Explainer: jam study presented as settled evidence of choice overload
column5: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd 2010 J Consumer Research 37:409 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/jconrs/v37y2010i3p409-425.html): 63 conditions/50 experiments, mean effect near zero, large between-study variance
column6: Added one hedge sentence after the jam result citing the 2010 meta-analysis; jam description itself unchanged

column2: Q0 expl.: "This pattern is remarkably stable across cultures and stakes"
column5: Same file's Explainer reports wide variation across 15 small-scale societies (Henrich et al. 2001, range 26-58%); Andersen et al. 2011 AER (https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:aea:aecrev:v:101:y:2011:i:7:p:3427-39): rejection of a given share falls as stakes rise
column6: Now "broadly stable across industrialized societies ... offers stay well above the minimum ... (though rejections of a given low share fall as stakes rise). Small-scale societies show much wider variation (Henrich et al.)."

column2: Explainer: "one of the most well-replicated ... findings"
column5: Plott & Zeiler 2005 AER found no WTA-WTP gap for mugs under controls for misconceptions; Isoni, Loomes & Sugden 2011 AER comment found the gap persists for lotteries (https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:aea:aecrev:v:101:y:2011:i:2:p:991-1011). Gap is widely documented but procedure-sensitive, so "well-replicated" unqualified overstates
column6: well-replicated -> "widely documented", plus a clause on procedure sensitivity (Plott-Zeiler mugs vs lotteries); "On the standard account," added before the loss-aversion reading

column2: Explainer para 2: "most automatically enrolled employees remaining at whatever rate and fund were selected as defaults"
column5: Madrian & Shea 2001 abstract (https://www.nber.org/papers/w7682): "a substantial fraction of 401(k) participants hired under automatic enrollment retain both the default contribution rate and fund allocation even though few employees hired before ... picked this particular outcome"; "most" with no time limit overstates (persistence decays over years)
column6: most ... remaining at whatever rate and fund -> "a substantial fraction ... remaining at both the rate and the fund selected as defaults, even though few employees hired before automatic enrollment had chosen that combination"

column2: Core Idea: "saliency (payoffs must be large enough to matter), dominance (reward structure dominates other motivations)"
column5: Smith 1982 AER precepts: saliency = rewards depend on subjects' actions via a known mapping; dominance = rewards large enough to outweigh other costs/motives (https://pauljhealy.github.io/ExpMethodsClass/01_vernon.pdf)
column6: Core Idea saliency/dominance definitions corrected; same misdefinition in Explainer para 2 ("large enough to matter (saliency)") corrected to "depend on your decisions (saliency) and are large enough to dominate other considerations (dominance)"

column2: Q1 expl.: "They persist among experts (physicians, statisticians)"
column5: Tversky & Kahneman 1981 Science report the reversal in groups including university faculty and physicians; no citable framing finding names statisticians (summary via search of 1981 paper; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framing_effect_(psychology) does not support statisticians)
column6: (physicians, statisticians) -> "(including physicians and university faculty)"; rest of sentence unchanged

column2: Q0 expl.: "the majority of employees remained in the default retirement plan years after enrollment, even when better-matched alternatives were available at no switching cost"
column5: Madrian & Shea 2001 abstract (https://www.nber.org/papers/w7682) supports "substantial fraction" keeping both defaults; their data cover recent hires, not "years after"; "better-matched alternatives at no switching cost" not stated in the paper
column6: Sentence now "a substantial fraction of employees hired under automatic enrollment kept both the default contribution rate and the default fund, even though they were free to change them and few employees hired before automatic enrollment had chosen that combination"

column2: Explainer para 2: "This pattern holds even when the stakes are raised to several months' wages"
column5: Andersen, Ertac, Gneezy, Hoffman & List 2011 AER (https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:aea:aecrev:v:101:y:2011:i:7:p:3427-39): proportionally equal offers are rejected less often at high stakes; offers remain above minimum
column6: Now "Offers stay well above the minimum even when the stakes are raised ... Rejection does respond to stakes, though: responders reject a given low share less often as the stakes rise."
